core/c1.A:
The weak point is the eight months. That's almost certainly eight months of living costs, and a bakery has a second bill that comes due before it sells anything: lease deposit, fit-out, ovens, mixers, refrigeration, permits, opening stock. In a space that wasn't already a commercial kitchen, that routinely runs into the tens of thousands. If it comes out of the same savings, you don't have eight months.

The clock also starts on the wrong day. It starts when the salary stops, not when the doors open, and finding a site, signing a lease, fitting it out and passing inspection usually takes a few months with nothing coming in. After opening, it's normal for a new food business to take a year or more to pay its owner a real wage. So the runway that counts is what's left after setup, divided by your monthly costs plus the bakery's monthly losses while it builds a customer base. Your own costs rise the day you leave, too, by everything your employer quietly pays for now, like health cover or pension contributions.

The lease is the part that can outlive the money. Commercial leases tend to run several years, and a landlord renting to a first-time owner will usually want a personal guarantee. A bakery that closes in month nine doesn't end the lease in month nine.

The plan also bundles two decisions: whether the bakery works, and whether to leave your job for it. Only the second needs you to quit. Most of what the eight months would buy you — whether people pay your prices often enough, and whether you like baking as production at four in the morning rather than as a craft — can be found out while you're still employed: a weekend market stall, wholesale to a couple of cafés, hours rented in a shared commercial kitchen, or selling from home where local cottage-food rules allow it. The expensive way to find out is month nine with a signed lease. The cheap way is a few months of Saturdays.
core/c1.B:
Eight months of savings isn't eight months of runway. The clock starts the day you quit, and a bakery earns nothing while you find a site, negotiate the lease, fit it out, and get through permits and a health inspection. That stretch is rarely shorter than a few months and often runs past six. The number that matters is how long you can last after the doors open, and every step on that list you get done before handing in your notice is time you're not paying for.

It also depends on what the eight months covers. If it's your living costs, the start-up money has to come from somewhere else, and bakeries are expensive to start: ovens, mixers, proofers, refrigeration, ventilation and the fit-out run to tens of thousands if you take over a space that was already a bakery, and well into six figures from a bare shell. The business needs its own cushion for the months it loses money, too. If one pot of savings is paying for all of that, eight months gets short fast. And your own costs rise once the job stops paying for things like health insurance or pension contributions.

The date the money has to reach isn't break-even. It's the first month the bakery can pay you. Those can be a long way apart: a bakery can cover its rent, flour and staff while the owner takes nothing home, and that's common for the first year or longer. A business can be on track and still run you out of money.

The downside isn't capped at your savings, either. Commercial leases run for years, and landlords usually want a personal guarantee from a first-time owner. Equipment finance often comes with one too. If the bakery closes in month ten, the lease doesn't. A stable job is usually easier to replace than a guaranteed lease is to get out of.

And running a bakery is mostly not baking. It's early mornings, food costs, staffing and unsold stock at closing time, with the baking fitted in around them. Most of what's uncertain here can be tested while you still have a salary: whether people pay your prices, how much you can turn out in a day, whether you like the work at that pace. Market stalls, supplying a café, a commercial kitchen rented by the hour, weekend shifts in someone else's bakery. If you've already been selling for a while, a lot of this is answered. If you haven't, the list of things you can only learn by quitting is short.
core/c1.C:
Counting it in months is the right instinct. The weak spot is what those eight months are measuring. If it's eight months of your own living costs, it doesn't cover the bakery itself: ovens, mixers, fit-out, deposits, permits, the first order of flour and butter. That's usually a separate pile of money, and a bigger one than people expect. If one pot of savings has to pay for both, you don't have eight months. You have whatever's left after you open.

The clock's tighter than it looks, too. It starts the day you quit, not the day you open, and finding a site, fitting it out and passing inspections can take months before you sell a single loaf. After that, it's normal for a new food business to take well over a year to cover its own costs, never mind pay its owner. So the number this really turns on isn't eight months of savings. It's how long you can go without a wage, from your last day at work to the first month the bakery pays you one.

And the worst case is bigger than losing the savings. Commercial leases tend to run for years, and for a first business the landlord will usually want a personal guarantee, so if the bakery shuts in month ten you can still owe rent for the rest of the term. Equipment finance often works the same way. That's the bit that turns an expensive experiment into something that follows you around.

None of this rules it out. The real choice just isn't bakery or no bakery, it's the order you do things in. Weekend markets, wholesale to a couple of cafés, or renting time in a shared commercial kitchen won't tell you everything a shop would. They will tell you the expensive part: whether enough people buy what you bake, at a price that covers ingredients, staff and rent, while your salary's still coming in.
core/c1.D: Eight months is the weak number. A new bakery often pays its owner nothing for a year or more. Start-up costs also land before the first sale: ovens, fit-out, permits, deposits, first stock. From savings, they shorten the eight months. From a loan, they add debt. The lease is the bigger risk. Commercial leases run for years. New tenants often have to sign a personal guarantee. That makes the rent your debt, not the bakery's. So the worst case isn't lost savings. It's years of rent on a closed shop. You can test the idea and keep the salary. Weekend markets and wholesale to cafés give you real sales at your prices. They also test the early starts and the volume.

core/c2.A:
A mandate is evidence of what executives believe, not of what's true about productivity. They have other reasons to want people back: leases they're still paying for, managers who judge work by watching it happen, and the fact that a mandate thins headcount without anyone paying severance. Ding and Ma's study of S&P 500 firms found mandates tended to follow a slump in the share price, and didn't improve performance afterwards. And a lot of what gets reported as return-to-office is three days a week, which is an odd way to act on the belief that remote days cost output.

The research itself splits by arrangement. Fully remote has a mixed record, with real productivity losses in several studies, from data entry to IT services. Hybrid mostly comes out neutral: in a randomised trial at Trip.com, published in Nature in 2024, two home days a week made no difference to performance reviews or promotions over two years, and cut quitting by about a third.

The best version of your argument is narrower. In a study of software engineers at a Fortune 500 firm, juniors who sat near their teammates got more feedback on their code, and the seniors giving it shipped less. That cost is real, and it lands on the newest people. It would also take years to show up in anyone's output, which is exactly where a productivity metric isn't looking.
core/c2.B: A mandate is evidence about executives, not about productivity. Executives also chose open-plan offices. The cleanest trial I know of ran at Trip.com. Two home days a week didn't lower performance. Quitting fell by a third. Fully remote is a different case, with real losses in several studies. And most of those orders are hybrid, not five days a week. That's close to the trial's setup.
core/c2.C:
The mandates are evidence about executives, not about output. Companies want people back for plenty of reasons that aren't productivity: a ten-year lease on a half-empty tower, managers who like seeing their teams, and the fact that a mandate thins headcount without anyone paying severance. The closest thing to a direct test I know of is Ding and Ma's study of S&P 500 firms. Mandates tended to follow a slump in the share price, financial performance didn't improve afterwards, and employee satisfaction fell. If offices were coming back because they make teams more productive, the results should have shown it.

"Every" doesn't hold either. Amazon and JPMorgan went to five days, but last I knew most of big tech had settled on three. That's a vote for hybrid, and two days at home is still remote work. Hybrid is also where the best evidence runs the other way. Nick Bloom's randomised trial at Trip.com gave graduate staff two home days a week. Performance reviews and promotions came out the same over the next two years, and quit rates fell by a third.

Your claim is strongest for fully remote work, and there it has real support. Data-entry workers in India randomly assigned to work from home were 18% less productive. Teams spread across distance produce fewer breakthrough papers and patents. Junior engineers get noticeably less feedback when they don't sit near their team. So fully remote costs something, mostly for juniors and for hard collaborative work. The five-day mandates, though, are mostly replacing hybrid, which is the arrangement with the best evidence behind it.
core/c2.D:
Reading what companies do instead of what they say is usually a good instinct. It just doesn't work here, because a return-to-office order tells you what executives believe, or want, and not what the productivity numbers show. Those two come apart. Big companies also went all-in on open-plan offices, mostly because they were cheaper per desk, and the research on those came back pretty unkind.

Plenty besides productivity pushes toward mandates: long leases on half-empty buildings, managers who'd rather manage people they can see, and the handy side effect that some people quit instead of coming back, which trims headcount without anyone announcing layoffs. And it isn't every big company. A lot of what gets called a return to the office is three days a week, which is hybrid.

That matters, because the studies I know of split along roughly the same line. Fully remote does show real costs in some jobs, and a lot of them land on junior people, since so much learning happens by overhearing and asking. Hybrid mostly shows no measurable hit to output, and fewer people quit. So there's something true in what you said. It's just narrower than “remote makes teams less productive,” and the mandates can't prove it either way.

core/c3.A:
Wanting the why is the right call, and not just on principle. It's what lets you rebuild a rule mid-exam when your memory goes blank.

Picture x² as the area of a square with side x. Stretch each side by a tiny amount, h. The new area is (x + h)² = x² + 2xh + h², so you've gained 2xh + h². In the picture, that's two thin strips along two edges, each x long and h wide, plus a little h-by-h square in the corner. The derivative asks how much area you gain per bit of side, so we divide by h and get 2x + h. Now let h shrink toward zero. The 2x stays put and the h vanishes. The 2 is there because a square grows along two edges at once. The corner drops out because it's small times small, so it fades much faster than the strips.

That method is the part worth owning: nudge the input, see what changes, divide by the nudge, let the nudge shrink. It's the actual definition of a derivative, and every rule you'll meet is this move with the working hidden. On a graph, the same fraction is the slope between two nearby points on the curve, and it becomes the slope of the tangent as they close in. A cube does the same thing with three faces growing at once, which is where the 3x² for x³ comes from. After that, the power rule stops being something you memorise and becomes something you could rebuild on the spot.
core/c3.B:
Picture a square with side x, so its area is x². Make the side a little longer, by a small amount h. The new area is (x + h)², and the extra comes in three pieces: a strip down one side (x by h), a strip along the top (x by h), and a little square in the corner (h by h). So the area grows by 2xh + h².

The derivative is the area gained per unit of length added, as the added length shrinks to nothing. Divide by h and you get 2x + h. Let h go to zero and you're left with 2x. That's exactly the limit of (f(x + h) − f(x)) / h in your textbook; the square is just that formula drawn.

Everything rests on dropping the corner, and "because it's tiny" isn't the reason. The strips are tiny too. What matters is how fast each piece shrinks. Halve h and the strips halve, but the corner quarters. Per unit of h, the strips are worth 2x however small h gets, while the corner is worth h, which goes to zero. A limit keeps the part that's proportional to h and throws away whatever shrinks faster.

The 2 isn't arbitrary either. It's the two edges the square grows along. A cube grows on three faces, each of area x², and the edge and corner bits vanish for the same reason as before, which is why x³ gives 3x². That's the power rule for whole-number powers, and the n out front is counting the same thing: how many directions the shape grows in.
core/c3.C:
Picture x^2 as an actual square with side x. The derivative is the rate its area grows as the side lengthens, which on the graph is the slope at that point.

Lengthen the side by a small amount h. The new area is (x + h)^2 = x^2 + 2xh + h^2, and every piece is visible: two thin strips along two edges, each x long and h wide, which make the 2xh, plus a tiny h-by-h square in the corner. Divide the added area by h to turn it into a rate and you get 2x + h. However small h gets, the strips still give you 2x. The corner gives you h, which shrinks to nothing. So the rate is exactly 2x. That's the formal definition, the limit of (f(x + h) - f(x))/h as h goes to 0, done with a picture. The 2 is there because two edges grow strips. The x is there because each strip is as long as the current side, so the same nudge adds more area to a bigger square.

At x = 3 the area is 9. At 3.001 it's 9.006001. That's 0.006001 of extra area for 0.001 of extra side, a rate of 6.001. The 6 is 2x, and the stray 0.001 is the corner: h^2 divided by h.

The same picture gives you the whole power rule. A cube of side x grows by three slabs, one on each of three faces, each x by x by h, so x^3 gives 3x^2. In general x^n is n copies of x multiplied together. Nudge any one copy, with the rest held fixed, and you add x^(n-1)·h; there are n copies to nudge. That's where "bring the exponent down and subtract one" comes from.
core/c3.D: A growing square gains area along two edges, each x long. Take a square of side x and area x². Lengthen the side by a tiny amount h. The area gains two x-by-h strips and one small h-by-h corner. That's 2xh + h² of new area. Divide by h for the change per unit of side: 2x + h. Now let h shrink to zero. The lone h disappears, leaving 2x. This is the limit definition of the derivative, or differentiating from first principles.

core/c4.A:
Liking it is the wrong test at this stage. You've read it so many times you're not reading it anymore — you're recognising it. You know every turn before it arrives and every joke is on its fortieth telling, so nothing in there can land on you. "I can't tell" is what that's like from the inside. It's a fact about how close you are to the book, not about the book.

There's one version of it that does mean something. If the whole thing's gone flat, that's familiarity. If you keep steering around one chapter, or a particular character makes you wince every time they open their mouth, that's a note, and a specific one.

What gets a reader's eyes back is time, not effort. A few weeks without opening it, then one quick read in a different format, printed or on an e-reader, without fixing anything as you go. And "anymore" means it worked on you once, before you knew it by heart.
core/c4.B:
“Can't tell” is the accurate way to put it. Past a certain number of rereads, you stop reading the book and start checking it against your memory of it. You know every turn before it comes, and a joke you've read thirty times isn't a joke anymore, so the part of you that would enjoy it as a reader has nothing left to work with. That says a lot about how many times you've been through it and very little about whether it's any good.

Distance is the usual fix. A few weeks in a drawer does more than any amount of staring. If you can't wait that long, you can fake it: change the font, print it out, read it aloud, or let your phone read it to you in that flat robot voice. Anything that makes it look like somebody else's manuscript gives you back a bit of a reader's eye.
core/c4.C:
Not being able to tell isn't the same as not liking it. The "anymore" matters: you liked it before you'd read it this many times. Past a certain number of rereads you can't experience a book the way a reader does, because you know every line before you reach it and nothing gets the chance to land. That flatness comes from familiarity. It isn't a verdict on the book.

Actual dislike tends to be specific — a character you're sick of, a chapter you dread opening — and that's real information. When it's just that you can't tell, the fixes are boring and they work: leave it alone for a few weeks, then read it in a form you've never seen it in, printed or on an e-reader or read aloud by text-to-speech, in as few sittings as you can. Or give it to one reader and have them mark where they got bored. That tells you more than anything they'll say about it afterwards.
core/c4.D: Months inside a book do that. Past a certain point you stop seeing the sentences. So not being able to tell isn't a verdict on the book. The standard fix is a few weeks away, then one straight read on paper. The dull stretches on that read are your real notes.

core/c5.A:
Weather is the state of the atmosphere at one place and time. Rain this afternoon. A cold week in March.

Climate is the statistics of weather over decades. The standard window is 30 years. It isn't just the average. It's the whole spread: the hottest days, the longest dry spells, the swing from one year to the next. One cold week is weather. A change in the number of cold weeks per decade is climate.

The deeper difference shows up in prediction. A weather forecast needs the exact state of the air right now. The atmosphere is chaotic: small errors in it grow fast. A tiny mistake in today's readings becomes a big one within days. So detailed forecasts give out at around two weeks. Climate doesn't need today's details. It's set by the planet's energy budget: sunlight in, heat out. Greenhouse gases hold back the heat going out. Nobody can forecast the rain on a given day in 2040. But the average summer of the 2040s can be estimated now.
core/c5.B:
Weather is the state of the atmosphere at one place and time. Today's rain. This afternoon's wind. Next Tuesday's heat.

Climate is the statistics of weather over decades. The standard window is 30 years. People often call it average weather. That's incomplete. Climate is the whole spread, not just the middle. Typical highs and lows. The number of floods. The worst heatwaves. The extremes do most of the damage. A small shift in the average makes them far more common.

The sharpest difference is in prediction. Weather forecasts stop being reliable after about ten days. The cause is chaos: tiny errors in today's measurements grow fast and swamp the forecast. Climate can still be projected decades out. That isn't a contradiction. A climate projection makes no claim about any particular day. It describes the shape of the spread. A single dice roll is unpredictable. The average of ten thousand rolls isn't. Loaded dice move that average in a predictable direction. Greenhouse gases are the loading.
core/c5.C: Weather is the state of the atmosphere at one place and time. Climate is the statistics of that weather over a long stretch, usually thirty years. That means the averages, the spread and the frequency of extremes. Weather forecasts fade after about ten days. Climate can be projected decades ahead. One predicts a particular day. The other predicts the odds.
core/c5.D:
Weather is the state of the air right now, in one place. Temperature, rain, wind, cloud. Climate is the long-run pattern of all that weather. The standard window is thirty years.

That's the timescale. It isn't the real difference. Climate isn't just an average. It's the full distribution: the odds of every kind of weather. How hot the hottest days get. How often it floods. How long the dry spells last. Weather is a single roll. Climate is the dice. On its own, a cold snap says nothing about climate. Thirty years of milder winters says a lot.

They're also different kinds of prediction. Weather is chaotic: tiny differences today grow into big ones next week. So day-by-day forecasts fade out after a week or two. Climate rests on something steadier. That's the energy balance: heat in from the sun against heat out to space. Shift that balance and you've loaded the dice. Nobody can call a single roll. You can still spot loaded dice.

core/c6.A:
Again is the hard part.

You had a reason each time. This result doesn't change the reason. It raises the cost of another try. That trade-off is real. The day of a result is a bad day to weigh it.

Later, the scores will tell you more than the pass or fail. Getting closer each time is one situation. The same score every time is a different one.
core/c6.B:
Sitting it again after failing takes more than sitting it the first time. You've already done that at least once. Something brought you back. There's your why, or part of it.

You don't have to decide about another attempt today. Right after a result is a bad time to judge all of it. The latest fail fills the whole view.

Later, putting the attempts side by side will tell you a lot. What moved between them. What stayed stuck. That can wait.
core/c6.C: That question can wait a week. Pass or fail is a blunt signal. The marks under it say much more. Two sets side by side show the stuck parts.
core/c6.D:
Twice is a lot.

That's a real question. Stopping is a real answer to it. So is going again. So is a break first. None of them has to be picked tonight. A result this fresh drowns out everything else.

logos/l1.A:
I'm having it built as a monthly recurrence: each month the balance earns a twelfth of the annual rate, then your deposit lands on top.

$$B_{t+1} = B_t\left(1 + \frac{r}{12}\right) + D$$

You'll be able to set the starting balance $B_0$, the deposit $D$, the rate $r$ and the number of months, and add what this plain version leaves out, like inflation, a deposit that rises with your pay, or tax on the interest. Then find the month where the interest alone first outgrows your deposit, and watch how far that month moves when you nudge the rate up a single point.
logos/l1.B: Building it as a balance that compounds monthly, $B_{t+1} = B_t\left(1+\frac{r}{12}\right) + D$: you can set the starting balance $B_0$, the monthly deposit $D$, the annual rate $r$ and the number of years, and move the deposit from the end of each month to the start.
logos/l1.C: What's being built is the balance month by month: each month it earns a twelfth of the annual rate, then your deposit lands on top, $B_{n+1} = B_n\left(1 + \tfrac{r}{12}\right) + D$. You'll be able to set the starting balance, the deposit, the rate and the number of years, and add what it leaves out, like inflation or a withdrawal. The part to distrust is $r$: it's held fixed for the whole horizon, and it's the one input that's a guess about the future rather than a choice you make. Once your numbers are in, halve the rate and see how much of the final balance goes with it — that's how much of the plan is resting on the guess.
logos/l1.D: I'm having it built as a month-by-month rule, $B_{t+1} = B_t\left(1 + \tfrac{r}{12}\right) + D$, with the starting balance $B_0$, the yearly rate $r$ and the monthly deposit $D$ all yours to set, and the compounding schedule is a piece you can swap if your bank doesn't do it monthly. Then here's a fun one: start from zero, find the month where the interest alone beats your deposit, and double $D$ to see whether that month budges at all.

logos/l2.A: *Obviously* is carrying that whole sentence, and the evidence won't hold it up. The best case on the other side: a randomized trial at Trip.com, published in Nature in 2024, found no difference in performance reviews or promotions between staff working two days a week from home and those in the office, and a third fewer of the hybrid group quit. Where losses do show up, it's mostly with fully remote work, or in the mentoring and cross-team contact that's hard to measure — real costs, but a narrower claim than the one you made. What result would change your mind?
logos/l2.B: It isn't *obvious*, and the people who have actually measured it don't agree with each other. Some studies find output falls, some find it rises, and a large randomised trial of hybrid work found no difference in performance at all. If you've watched a particular team slow down, that's worth taking apart, but it's a claim about that team and that kind of work, not a law.
logos/l2.C: Not *obviously*. The evidence splits by setup: hybrid arrangements mostly show no drop in performance, while some fully remote studies do find real productivity losses. What holds up better is narrower — newer people tend to get less feedback and mentoring away from colleagues — so the claim you can defend depends on which teams and what kind of productivity you mean.
logos/l2.D: That *obviously* is carrying a lot for a question researchers are still openly fighting over — in one of the best-known experiments, call-centre staff randomly assigned to work from home actually got more done. Funny thing is, your strongest word is 'teams': where the evidence does back you is the collaborative stuff, like junior people getting less feedback and cross-team conversations quietly thinning out. Drop the 'obviously', lean on the 'teams', and you've got a claim that's a lot harder to knock down.

logos/l3.A: *Always* is where it breaks. It's what the competitive-market model predicts, but that's one model, not all of economics: where employers have the power to set wages (monopsony), a modest minimum can raise employment. And two of the most-cited studies of real increases — Card and Krueger's New Jersey fast-food study, and a 2019 analysis of 138 US state increases — found little or no loss of jobs. The defensible version of your view is narrower: push the minimum high enough relative to local wages and losses become likely, though nobody can say exactly where that line is. What result would make you drop the "always"?
logos/l3.B: That's one textbook model, not the whole of economics: the competitive case predicts job losses, but where employers have wage-setting power a moderate minimum can leave employment flat or even raise it, and the evidence since Card and Krueger's 1994 fast-food study is genuinely split. What does hold up is that size matters — a minimum close to the local median wage is far more likely to cost jobs than a modest one — so *always* is the word that fails.
logos/l3.C: 'Always' is where this breaks, and the twist is that economics is what breaks it. The textbook supply-and-demand model does predict job losses, but monopsony models, where employers have real power over wages, say a modest rise can leave employment flat or even nudge it up — and plenty of the evidence since Card and Krueger's 1994 fast-food study finds small or no losses from moderate increases. Take it to the absurd end, a hundred-dollar minimum wage, and you'd be dead right, which tells you the claim worth defending is about *how much*, not whether.
logos/l3.D: That's one model in economics, not economics. The textbook supply-and-demand version predicts job losses because it assumes employers have no power over wages; where they do have that power, a modest increase can leave employment flat or even raise it, and the evidence since Card and Krueger's New Jersey study has been argued in both directions. What economists actually disagree about is how big an increase has to be, relative to local wages, before the losses show up, and *always* skips that question entirely.

logos/l4.A: Nothing you've said is about the job itself. Would you want it if it paid exactly what you earn now, or is the money doing all the pulling?
logos/l4.B: Here's what jumps out: the job itself, and the city you'd be moving to, don't come up at all. So a what-if — if the same money turned up tomorrow without you having to move an inch, would there be anything left to decide?
logos/l4.C: "More money" is the only part of this without a number on it, and it's the part being asked to outweigh your friends — so before it gets weighed at all, it has to survive the new city's cost of living and what it costs to keep coming back. Here's a test: if the offer paid exactly what you earn now, would you still be tempted? If you would, the money isn't really what's pulling you, and it's worth knowing what is.
logos/l4.D: It turns on three things the money-versus-friends framing hides: what the raise actually buys once the new city's costs come out of it, which of these friendships would survive the distance rather than fade without proximity, and whether the job itself is a step forward or just better paid.

logos/l5.A:
It's the probability of getting a result at least as extreme as yours, *assuming* the null hypothesis is true:

$$p = P(\text{data at least this extreme} \mid H_0)$$

So it tells you how surprising your data would be in a world where the effect doesn't exist, not how likely that world is given your data. Reading $p = 0.03$ as a 3% chance the null is true flips the conditional, and turning one into the other needs a prior the p-value never had.
logos/l5.B: It's the probability of getting a result at least as extreme as yours *if* the null hypothesis (usually "no effect") were true: $p = P(\text{result at least this extreme} \mid H_0)$. That "if" is where it usually gets misread: the calculation assumes nothing is going on, so it can't also tell you the chance that nothing is going on, which is why $p = 0.03$ does not mean a 3% chance the finding is a fluke. It doesn't measure the size of the effect either — with enough data, a trivially small effect gets a tiny p-value — and the 0.05 line it's usually judged against is a convention, not something anyone measured.
logos/l5.C: It's the probability of a result at least as extreme as yours *if* the null hypothesis were true — $P(\text{data this extreme} \mid H_0)$, the share of the null distribution lying at least as far out as your test statistic. It is not the chance the null is true, $P(H_0 \mid \text{data})$: it tells you how surprising your data would be in a world where the null holds, not how likely that world is.
logos/l5.D: It's the answer to a slightly backwards question: if nothing interesting were going on (that's the null hypothesis), how often would plain chance hand you a result at least as extreme as yours? Say a coin you suspect is rigged lands heads 9 times out of 10 — a fair coin does something that lopsided, 9 or more of either face, with probability $\tfrac{22}{1024} \approx 0.02$, so that's your p-value. The bit that trips up even working scientists is the direction: it's $P(\text{data this extreme} \mid H_0)$, *not* $P(H_0 \mid \text{data})$, so it's never the chance the null is true, or that your result was just a fluke.
